segments.text: Ladies and gentlemen, I will invite the moderator, who will in turn invite her panelists. Please join me as I welcome Dr. Francesca Giovannini . Good morning, everyone.

I, in particular, want to welcome our young talents. I very much look forward to our youth discussion. I'm a professor at Harvard University, and so I really look forward to engaging with this wonderful talent in a few minutes.

But I am particularly honored to have the chance to moderate a session that I consider to be quite revolutionary. Chairman of the Rwanda Atomic Energy Board and President Kagame both said that Africa is really facing a historical moment. In fact, I think it's fair to say that the global nuclear energy landscape is really facing an unprecedented, unprecedented revolutionary age.

Now, we know that the case for nuclear energy in Africa has been made, and I think it is incredibly solid and very credible. But for a long time, only a few actors played in this space, mostly government and nuclear suppliers. Recently, multilateral financial institutions decided to join in investments and in research and development.

But there is a fourth actor, a key player that for many years shaped many critical domains. If I ask you, the Gates Foundation, I'm pretty sure you understand the Gates Foundation has shaped, together with governments and multilateral institutions, the healthcare system. So the philanthropy space is not only a partner, it is a strategic shaker and mover in any space it operates.

And therefore, I am particularly pleased that we've launched on Monday, and we will actually dig more into it today, the Global Coalition for Nuclear Philanthropy. If you think about the role the Carnegie Foundation, the MacArthur Foundation have played in many fields, you can imagine what these foundations can do for the nuclear energy sector in the future. To get this conversation going, I'm very honored to have with me the architects and the designers of this Global Coalition for Nuclear Philanthropy.

It has taken a long journey. They've worked very, very hard to put it together, to create the momentum. And they are here at NEISA to engage in a conversation about why these big players are getting into this field? Why now and why in Africa? Let me join my panelist,Karen Hallberg ,who is Secretary General, Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs
Shunando Basu, who is the Director of Energy, Technology and Innovation for the Rockefeller Foundation.Dr. Sama Bilbao y León Director General, World Nuclear Association (WNA
First of all, I am so grateful and excited to have you.

Because it's not every day that an organization that has done different work decides in a way to add a new strategic domain in their portfolio. So it is obvious to ask the first question. And I want to start with you, Shunando, as the Rockefeller Foundation, who is going to be one of the biggest shapers in this field.

What did you see to decide this was the moment to enter into the nuclear field? Thank you, Francesca. Thank you for having me and thank you to all of you. Thank you to NEISA for inviting us and it's an honor to be on the stage to speak about the work that the Rockefeller Foundation is doing in nuclear space.

So let me start by saying that everything that we're doing at the Rockefeller Foundation from the power and energy team is really centered around the concept of universal energy abundance. The fact that energy should be accessible, affordable, and abundant all around the world, right? And as part of this, we have many things that we do from Mission 300, which aims to electrify 300 million people across Africa by 2030. But there's another side to this, right? And we've been hearing about this extensively all throughout so far here at NEISA, which is that for real socioeconomic growth, for increasing and improving the industrial base of African countries, you need an actual step change in the availability of electricity.

And that is precisely what we believe that nuclear energy has the potential to do. And so that's why from the Rockefeller side, we decided that this is something that's important and this is something that we need to back and that it requires a lot of philanthropic intervention and coordination across a lot of different sectors. Terrific.
You have worked very closely with Karen. You two have been really the architects, the drivers, the shakers together with Tomasic Trust. So let me go to you, Karen.

First of all, I also would like you to reflect a little bit about this moment, why the Oppenheimer Project is in fact being involved in this. But also could you clarify a little bit for the audience what do we mean by philanthropy? So is Elon Musk involved in this? So give us a sense of how you define philanthropy. Thank you, Francesca, and thank you for having me here, my second time at NEISA.

And I have to say when we actually met, Shunando and I met here in person for the first time in Kigali last year. And that was the beginning of our journey of working together. Oppenheimer Project is a nonprofit organization honoring the legacy of the late Dr. Robert Oppenheimer, a grandfather of my husband, Charles, who you saw in the video earlier.

And we started working in nuclear energy as a, we wanted to focus on nuclear technology as a source for hope. And found that the Oppenheimer name and brand and legacy could lend a kind of trusted voice to the space as many of us know, it's a kind of difficult topic. And we found ourselves coming in and creating dialogue has been surprisingly effective.

And so we met the Rockefeller Foundation, started talking about this a year ago. And in between the last NEISA and now, we convened a few workshops, convening Sama was a part of that and a few others in the room to talk about the role of philanthropy. And your question, philanthropy.

Philanthropy is provided like a trusted voice and neutral voice with public interest in mind. So the difference between the public sector, private sector, and then philanthropy. Yes, a lot of the money behind philanthropy comes from successful entrepreneurs and business people like Bill Gates, like the Rockefellers.

But really when they said that word, actually, I don't know the definition of philanthropy, I should have looked it up, the actual dictionary definition, but really it's about public good. And when we say philanthropy is important as a key player in this, it really means that philanthropy is supporting civil society. And so many organizations are funded by member states, by industry, they all serve a purpose, but civil society represents public good and public interest.

So that's where philanthropy is important. Before I go into the goals of the coalition and how you think you are going to play this sort of movement, I wanted to ask Dr.Sama a question that builds on what Canon said.
It's very true that philanthropy can in a way demystify the question of nuclear. There's a lot of politics. Every time people think about nuclear is always anti-nuclear or pro-nuclear.

Could you, you have been involved in this field for a long time. What do you think is the influence of more neutral parties that said we have the public interest in mind and this is why we're here? How important is it in your view to depoliticize the issue a little bit , Well, first of all, once again, it is a pleasure to be here today with all of you and I'm so excited that we have been able to announce this global coalition this week. It is so synergistic to do it in NEISA and also come to Africa.

I think it's fabulous to see the global importance of this opportunity. So to your question, Francesca, I think it's so important and certainly I think has made a difference from our work to have an unbiased voice, somebody that is not perceived to have a personal interest or a company interest or an institutional interest on explaining how, well, in this case, nuclear energy is absolutely essential for providing, well, as you said, energy abundance for prosperity, for growth, for development, for quality of life everywhere in the world. So on our side, I mean, so for many years, our Nuclear Association has been working with many, sometimes philanthropic, sometimes UN organizations and we were trying to do our work without putting our name anywhere because that gave so much credibility.

I mean, so if you produce a report where you explain how nuclear does this, that or the other thing, and you say, by the World Nuclear Association, well, what else are you going to say, right? But if this is a report that is produced by the Rockefeller Foundation of the United Nations or somebody else, it's a whole different thing. So I think it's essential to bring, as you said, this civil interest, social interest, unbiased point of view, just bringing the facts to the people and I think that philanthropy is going to be essential for that. Terrific.

So I want to dig a little bit into what you plan to do. Let me say that this global coalition is also challenging something I didn't know I learned from them, in fact, that the majority of the funds that go into the field is actually directed towards nuclear non-proliferation. And there's almost nothing in the civil society space that in fact supports instead, really more investments, more capacity building on the nuclear energy side.

And so it is a game changer. So we want to understand a little bit more about this. Shenandoah, could you tell us a little bit whether, what are the strategic priorities? How long does the first initial phase go? How do you plan to work together? Give us a little bit more details.

Yeah, of course. Yeah, happy to dig into this a bit. So since you brought up the topic of dollars going into space, I want to throw a statistic out there, right? So climate philanthropy is historically underestimated, under-invested in nuclear significantly by a really wide margin with less than $2 for every thousand that goes into the space being allocated to nuclear.

So this is a major gap that we are hoping to address with the creation of the coalition, right? The second thing that's really important is that for nuclear energy to be a reality in the next say 10 to 15 years, we need to double the amount of dollars that goes into the space to between 125 and $150 billion, right? That's almost three times the amount that's going in to the space today. And so those dollars aren't going to come from philanthropy directly. That is not what I'm trying to say, but what we can do is be catalytic in our actions, right? And what I mean by that is to fund a lot of the upstream pre-commercial work that will enable the ecosystem to absorb those dollars that will hopefully come from multilateral institutions and governments and banks and the private sector as well, right? It's important that we create things like blended finance instruments, first loss funds.

And that's precisely what we are hoping to do with what we're calling the make it bankable pathway. That is one of the four pillars of the Global Coalition for Nuclear Philanthropy. And that's precisely what we're hoping to do.
Terrific. Karen, you have some strategic areas. You will also operate a secretariat.

Tell us a little bit more about what you think, how, what are going to be your priorities moving forward and how are you going to work with all these foundations joining? We, as you saw in the opening slide, there are Rockefeller Foundation and domestic trusts are kind of the elites. Yes, the three organizations have been sort of the architect of this, but we brought on five other founding members and those organizations, those foundations are actually philanthropies who've actually been funding in the nuclear energy space for quite a while. Most of them have been focused on US policy and it's actually made some great strides.

And we developed a project, a little field guide for philanthropy to highlight the case that philanthropy can make a difference. And we have stopped a nuclear power plant in California from shutting down with pretty small dollars, really supporting advocates and policy advocacy, both policy advocacy and grassroots and commissioning a study to show the importance of this one power plant called Diablo Canyon. That's just an example of things.

So we're continuing to use this platform to kind of educate, but also bring in more members and more members, meaning more dollars, hopefully going into supporting civil society efforts. I think we spent the last year thinking through, one of the questions we get asked a lot is, why do we need philanthropy in the public and private sector and the dollar amounts that Shenandoah just mentioned, like what can philanthropy do? So we did, Shenandoah you mentioned one of the areas, which is around like unlocking financing. And we heard yesterday and throughout the conference about financing.

And if you remember, we actually got back down to regional cooperation. How do we pull risk and build trust and legitimacy? And there are a lot of upstream work other than putting actual money into projects that can be done. So that's one area.
The other three pillars are building the case, continuing to support the storytelling. It's a pretty brittle field. If we have one accident tomorrow, we're gonna set ourselves back many, steps.
We've been sticking for a long time to get to where we are now. So we need philanthropic support to continue to fund that kind of polling and building the evidence. And growing the field.
We heard about the youth. That's one area. How do we support the next generation? But it's not just about the workforce.

Future workforce is all about current policymakers and institutional capacity. How do we build the right institutions so that they can unlock financing, so that they build expertise. And the fourth area is strengthening governance.

So we have IEA here and WNA, and they are over capacity. There's so much interest in nuclear right now, so how do we support these institutions to continue to do what they do well? Fantastic. This is a great segue to a question I have for you, Sama, because Karen said there is so much interest in nuclear.

It is obvious that organizations like you, as much as you can work hard, you will reach a point where you won't be able to respond to demand. Could you reflect a little bit on how you're coping with this? And how do you see the coalition really helping, filling this demand that cannot be managed? Well, you're right. I mean, I think that is not too much demand.

There is never too much. I think it's great that we have new countries, new regions, new parts of the world that are very interested in learning about nuclear. But for us, so World Nuclear Association, we are a global organization of industry members.

And historically, in the last few years, we had maybe one or two countries per year that would come and tell us, Poland wanted to learn what would it take to, yes, they've been working with the IEA, they know the milestones process, but they really wanted to understand, now what? How do I bring industry? How do I actually realize this thing? But it was one country, Poland. One country was Kazakhstan. But right now, we have the entire ASEAN region.

So this is what, 11 countries that are very interested in understanding this, the entire African region. So it's simply, well, we would have to triple our size to be able to meet the needs that these countries have. And frankly, I think that there is also the coordination point of view, right? Actually, even though each region and each country definitely has nuances and things that make them different, working together can actually help do that.

So I think that philanthropy is going to be very supportive to the work that we are doing, trying to, as you said, sustain and enhance and make sure that we continue to be able to do this with the quality and the depth that we've been doing for, obviously, many years. Fantastic. Now, I have a question, because it might sound obvious that foundations have money, they've come to Africa, why not invest? But there's a lot of learning for these foundations.

It's rather obvious they know how Rwanda works. What is the grid capacity in Africa? And so I know, Shenandoah and Karen, you have done a lot of learning. I know, Shunando, you've been here last year, you've been this year, you've had a lot of meetings to understand a little bit what is the landscape.

Tell us what are the things that you would like to know or that you think you want to access to make decisions, because you have never worked in this field, at least in Africa. And so this is a completely new landscape, these are new partners for you, and you are also new to the field. So what would you say are the key things that you need to know about getting into this space? And how can these African countries help you getting access to the information you need? That's a great question, Francesca.

So coming to conferences just like this one, to NEISA between last year and this year, I mean, I cannot tell you the amount I learned from coming here last year, because that is actually what enabled me to then go back to New York and then tell my leadership that, hey, listen, we need to seriously think about some thought leadership that we can get out in this space. And I still remember to this day, Sam, it was with you out on that terrace last year, talking to you saying, you know what, we need to get a study out there that finally dispels this notion that nuclear is too expensive for emerging markets. And we did exactly that in November, we published the study, and I encourage all of you to read it if you haven't read it already.

But that kind of learning is exactly what I can, I mean, I personally need to continue doing. And as a philanthropic sector, I think we are going to do collectively, right, to get hopefully more support in the space overall. And to all African leaders who are out there today, the one thing I kindly ask of you is that you give us that bandwidth and that opportunity to keep having conversations with you, to keep learning.

Certainly, I've been doing some of that here this year as well, and I hope to continue doing that so that we can figure out and really pinpoint what the enabling factors are, right? Like, what do we need to do to make sure that we are unlocking the right things, right? Whether it's unlocking finance, making sure we're getting the right technical assistance in place, getting regulatory assistance in place. These are all activities that the Rockefeller Foundation is hoping to do as part of this. Terrific.

Karen, could you comment as well on this? You know, the role that it really brings to, like what the coalition will do, and I think the reason we built a coalition and not just have Rockefeller and the other members kind of go at this kind of individually is that we can collectively learn. And we need a lot of funding, as we already said, in this space, but we want to spend it the right way. It's not about the dollar amount.

Some people say, oh, tripling nuclear, so you should triple philanthropy. I'm like, well, what does tripling actually mean? Where is that money going? So I think there is a lot for us to learn to make sure the dollars we put in and the organizations we support are impactful. And for that, we have to, I think our role as a project has been connecting the dots.

That's what we do. We build bridges, we connect with experts, and we kind of piece it all together and say, well, what are some fundable, like philanthropically fundable kind of solutions? And we're gonna spend the next year doing just that, bringing, sourcing solutions, asking the community to send us ideas so that we can learn. And hopefully in the next year, we're definitely planning on deploying more funding, not just sitting there navel gazed and learn everything we want.
But learn and also deploy at the same time. So. It's not my money, but I was trying to channel the money.

These are the real deal, people. Sama, I wanted to ask you to reflect a little bit. So you have a pretty extraordinary, very comprehensive understanding of the nuclear landscape, right? So the governments, you have been dealing with all sorts of players.

Where do you see philanthropy fitting? Well, I think that there are many places. I mean, and of course, we have done, you have done a lot of work to find out what those are. I think that many of us in the nuclear community, probably in the back of our minds or sometimes in the front of our minds, have ideas, oh, if I had the resources, I could do this, I could work with those people, we could connect those dogs.

So there are many things that we simply were not able to do because, well, we didn't have the resources and because they were not the number one priority, not to say that they were not just as important and potentially as impactful. So I think that this is where philanthropy can help us to actually do things that perhaps we were never able to do together because we're not the immediate, urgent thing that needed to be done. So that is one thing.

And then what I think is the very important part that both Fernando and Karen mentioned is the catalytic aspect. So there's going to be some amount of financial support that is going to come from philanthropy, hopefully a lot, but that's not even the point. The point is how we can maximize the impact of that amount of money, amount of resources to actually reach, well, these big goals that we all have.

So that's how I see it. And Karen mentioned some of the areas, whether it is education, whether it is information, whether it is maintaining, explaining all the time and more clearly articulating better the story about nuclear and maintaining the institutions, the leadership, the know-how, not just the technical know-how, but also the leadership that we needed in the nuclear industry. So there's many things that we can do, so I'm excited about this.

Yes. And just on that point, I think philanthropy, the storytelling and educating, the trust, credibility and legitimacy is so important right now, continue to be. Like I said, this story of nuclear is kind of brittle, and so we need to, and I think that's where philanthropy, philanthropically supported messaging is really important.

Right, I have a question, and I want to ask it on behalf of the young people, because, you know, and we'll talk in the next panel, your career trajectory is also going to be shaped by the opportunities that emerge, like this one. You know, when I started university, nobody was talking about nuclear, right? In Europe, it was all about renewables and so on and so forth, so I would have never thought about a career in nuclear energy. But today, you are really in that historical moment where these opportunities are emerging, and some of them will shape your career.

But if I were a young, you know, student today, sitting in this audience, my concern would be, yeah, but these are big foundations, why would they care about me, right? So maybe you will end up working with the super fancy think tank in Washington, DC, you know, to do one of the studies that nobody will ever read, and so, like, it won't change very much the equation for me. So we've talked a little bit in NEISA this year also about localization, and making sure the money is actually invested where it's needed, and not to the fancy think tanks in Washington. Shenandoah, to you, like, how are you guys thinking about localization? So we want to make sure that as many dollars as possible that are deployed come to Africa and the rest of the Global South.

That is very, very much the goal, and it's also very much in line with the ethos of the Rockefeller Foundation and the way that we operate, right? And on that thread also, I want to add that we always seek out partnership, but not just any, just partnership generally, but partnership on equal terms, right? Making sure that the groups that we work with are also stakeholders in the work that we do and feel included in the process and feel like that they are genuinely contributing and are partnering with us on the work, right? So going back to your question about youth, right? This is, I think, that the nuclear sector, I think over the next decade, decade and a half, is going to be an area of immense opportunity, right? And I really hope all of you out there that are part of these various youth movements that I'm so, so excited about, my goal is to get you excited as well and keep you excited and make sure that we can include you in the work that we seek to do in the nuclear space. Garrett, do you want to comment a little bit on localization? Yeah, I mean, I came from global health and development for a couple of decades, and the one thing I did not see a lot sometimes is like, you know, we're not people and community centered in the way we think about how the funding and the work impacts the people who are impacted most. So, I mean, Shenandoah already said that, you know, the idea that we will, it is about, you know, we're not going to sit in San Francisco and New York and decide what is best.
We're triangulating. I said, connect the dots. We take what we hear here, all the connections, and we piece together, you know, something that would, that makes sense for philanthropy.
And so we're not there deciding what's important. And yeah. Terrific.

Before I close, I want to use the method that was used in the opening panel at NEISA 2026. And I actually want you to commit to a resolution. Most importantly, I want to ask in a year from now, how would we assess success? Noting that success is long-term, is slow, but what would be something that within the 12 months you would like to accomplish that you are going to present at NEISA 2027 that would celebrate? Whoever wants to start.

Salwa. Well, you know, I do have many goals, but I think it would be good if focusing specifically on philanthropy. I think that we have some visibility of some things that we could do relatively soon in Africa to catalyze.

I mean, there is enormous momentum, but we still need to catalyze it. We really need to put in place or help accelerate putting in place some of this infrastructure, whether it's regulatory, whether it's workforce, et cetera, et cetera. So maybe we can come up next year to show what we have done specifically to help accelerate some of those things with these philanthropic efforts.

I think I have a couple of points on this one. And really quick, because I also covered this as well, I think a really measurable success point would be some improvement in utility power grids, right? That is my other area of focus at RF. And if we can concretely say that we helped at least some number of utilities in Africa improve their overall state of health and performance, I think that would be a fantastic measurable outcome.

And that's all in partnership with the Global Energy Alliance. The second thing I'll say really quickly is hopefully being able to get some countries further along the IEA milestones process. That is something that we discussed extensively at our convening that we had last fall, hosted by us with our various philanthropic partners.

So if we can help countries make progress along that process, I think that would also be a very successful measurable outcome. From the coalition's point of view, I think we wanna grow, we wanna bring more members in, but really the statistic that Shunando gave about how little funding is in nuclear energy, the percentage is 0.2% applying to philanthropy. We wanna see that increase.

But I also wanna make sure that we bring more funding partners like the Rockefeller Foundation that has a focus on this geography. As I said, many of them are focused on US policy, but those foundations have some interest, but they have a lot to learn. So I hope next year when we come back, we can say that we have unlocked more funding and more philanthropies who want to contribute in this space.

Well, it's obvious that NEISA is both aspirational and very pragmatic, but it's fundamental to have a vision. And you started with a vision, you have been able to bring it to a concrete outcome. This global coalition has the chance to shape a lot of really critical decisions and debates, and you are the right people to lead this.
Thank you very much. Thank you. Over to you.
